airport.name: Point Lonely Short Range Radar Site Airfield

summary: Point Lonely Short Range Radar Site Airfield is a remote airstrip situated on Alaska's Arctic North Slope near the Beaufort Sea coast. The airfield primarily supports a military radar installation, part of the regional air defense network monitoring Arctic airspace. Its extreme northern location and isolation make it accessible mainly to personnel and supply aircraft.
faqs:
Q: What is the primary purpose of Point Lonely Airfield?
A: The airfield supports a Short Range Radar Site, part of Alaska's air defense infrastructure monitoring Arctic airspace for the North Warning System.

Q: Is Point Lonely Airfield open to civilian travelers?
A: No, this is a restricted-use airfield serving military and support personnel only. Public access is not available.

Q: What aircraft typically use this airfield?
A: Small military transport aircraft, such as C-12 Huron and similar types, commonly use the airstrip along with occasional larger cargo planes delivering supplies.

Q: How remote is Point Lonely?
A: The airfield is located approximately 70 degrees north latitude on the Arctic coastal plain, hundreds of miles from the nearest road-connected community.
transport_tips: Access to Point Lonely is by air only, as there are no roads connecting this site to the rest of Alaska. Flights typically originate from Fairbanks or Deadhorse (Prudhoe Bay), and visitors must have prior authorization for landing. Travelers should coordinate logistics well in advance and prepare for limited or no ground transportation upon arrival.
local_tip: Pack for extreme Arctic conditions regardless of season—summer temperatures can still hover around freezing, and winter brings polar darkness with lows well below -40°F. Bring layered clothing, headlamps useful during the long dark months, and any personal medications, as resupply options are extremely limited.
